originalTitle: Notes from a nursing home: ‘Our books told of who we were. The story of us. Then the movers came and asked what should go’
summary: Pencil marks in the margins of books gathered over a lifetime was proof of a life lived. So when it came time for Andrew McKean to move into aged care, leaving his books behind made the self thinner
content: My wife, Patricia, and I came to our nursing home with little more than clothes, a few photographs and some books we could still carry. The shelves we left behind still stand in the emptied rooms of the house we called home for 30 years. Those shelves once groaned under the weight of books we had gathered, page by page, year by year. Our books told of who we were, or who we thought we might become. There were the novels Patricia read in the long evenings after the children slept, their spines cracked from her hands. There were the histories I brought home from the library sales, dusty volumes of wars and voyages that filled the quiet hours when rain beat on the roof. Poetry too, slim books with thin paper, marked where a line struck true. We kept them not only for the stories printed inside but for the story they made of us. The day came when the movers stood in the doorway and asked what should go. We had known it would come. The nursing home allows only a small cabinet beside the bed. Four or five volumes at most. The rest must be given away or sold or simply left for strangers to claim. Patricia sat in the armchair and looked at the ranks of titles as though they were faces she would not see again. I walked the length of the shelves and touched the backs of books I had not opened in decades. What struck hardest were the notes in the margins. In one novel of mine a pencil mark still shows where I disagreed with the hero’s choice. In Patricia’s copy of a memoir, she had written a single word beside a paragraph about loss. That word was “yes”. Elsewhere a date appears in the corner of a page, the day we first read it together by the fire. Those marks were private conversations with the print, small proofs that we had lived inside those pages. To give the books away was to give away the proof. We packed a few to keep. One slim volume of poems for Patricia, the one she could recite without looking. One fat history for me, its maps still folded at the end, and a precious paperback of James Joyce, Dubliners, where in Araby the unnamed adult narrator describes the former tenant of Joyce’s childhood home, a priest, who died there, and left behind a few paper-covered books, the pages of which were curled and damp: The Abbot, by Walter Scott, The Devout Communicant, and The Memoirs of Vidocq. The rest of our books went into boxes. I remember the sound of the tape sealing those boxes. It was a dry, final sound. Patricia did not cry, but her hands stayed on the last shelf longer than they needed to. Leaving the books was leaving the rooms where we had been younger. The chairs by the window, the lamp that threw a circle of light on the open page, the habit of reaching for a particular volume when the day turned sour. Those habits formed a kind of self. Without the shelves the self felt thinner. Who was the man who once knew the order of every title? That man stayed behind with the books. The man who walks the corridor of the nursing home is a smaller edition, abridged. Yet here, though our room holds so little space for our own, the common rooms carry shelves stacked high with books left by those who came before us. Volumes of every kind lean together, novels and histories and poems, their pages turned by many hands. Anyone may take them, read them, return them. They are not ours, and the margins hold no marks of ours, yet they stand open for the days that remain. I can still close my eyes and see the blue spine of the travel book we bought the year we thought we might cross the sea. I can hear Patricia’s voice reading aloud from the novel she loved best. The margins we marked are gone, but the memory of marking them is not. In this narrow room the few books we kept lean against each other on the cabinet. When I open one I find the old pencil lines still speaking of the hours we spent with them. The print is the same. Only the room has changed, and the man who holds the book. • Andrew McKean is a writer and a resident of an aged care facility in New South Wales, Australia
chineseTitle: 来自疗养院的笔记：“我们的书讲述了我们是谁。我们的故事。然后搬家工人过来询问该走什么”
chineseSummary: 一生中收集的书籍页边的铅笔痕迹是生活的证明。因此，当安德鲁·麦基恩 (Andrew McKean) 进入老年护理行业时，把他的书抛在脑后让他的自我变得更薄弱。
chineseContent: 我和妻子帕特里夏来到疗养院时只带了衣服、几张照片和一些我们还可以携带的书。我们留下的架子仍然矗立在我们称之为家 30 年的房子的空房间里。那些书架曾经在我们一页一页、一年一年地收集的书籍的重压下发出呻吟声。我们的书讲述了我们是谁，或者我们认为自己可能成为谁。孩子们入睡后，帕特里夏在漫长的夜晚读小说，书脊从她手中折断。我从图书馆的销售中带回了一些历史书，尘土飞扬的战争和航海书籍，充满了雨打在屋顶上的安静时光。诗歌也是如此，薄薄的书本，薄薄的纸张，标明了其中的一句台词。我们保留它们不仅是因为里面印有故事，也是因为它们讲述了我们的故事。有一天，搬家工人站在门口询问应该搬什么。我们就知道它会来。疗养院只允许在床边放一个小柜子。最多四五卷。其余的必须赠送或出售或干脆留给陌生人领取。帕特里夏坐在扶手椅上，看着一排排头衔，仿佛这些面孔是她再也见不到的了。我沿着书架走过去，摸了摸几十年来没有打开过的书的书背。最引人注目的是页边空白处的注释。在我的一本小说中，铅笔标记仍然表明我不同意主人公的选择。在帕特里夏的回忆录中，她在一段关于失去的段落旁边写了一个词。这个词是“是”。在其他地方，页面的一角出现了日期，即我们第一次在火边一起阅读的那天。这些标记是与印刷品的私人对话，是我们生活在这些页面中的小证据。把书送出去是
